summary: Defines a Management Information Base extension to Remote Monitoring that lets the interfaces of a monitored device be sorted by interface-specific parameter values.

eli5.summary: It lets a network watcher line up a machine's plugs from busiest to quietest.

questions: what is a top n report
subtitle: An RMON extension that ranks a device's interfaces by a chosen counter, so managers see the busiest or most troubled ports first.

tldr.problem: Switches and routers can have hundreds of ports with tens of counters each, so a monitoring application cannot easily show which interfaces are congested or problematic.
tldr.mechanism: The InterfaceTopN MIB lets a management station create a report that samples one chosen interface object over a time interval and lists the top N interfaces in decreasing order of value, optionally normalized for different interface speeds.
tldr.outcome: A short ranked list replaces the full set of counters. A manager could, for example, copy the top interface to a port with a network analyzer attached. It is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement.

today: RFC 3144 is a Proposed Standard, published in August 2001. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Rank Interfaces
sections.content:
RFC 3144 defines a piece of the Management Information Base (MIB) that extends Remote Monitoring (RMON). It continues the architecture of the RMON MIB (RFC 2819) and the SMON MIB (RFC 2613) by adding a method to order a device's interfaces by the value of a specific parameter.

The need comes from devices such as bridges and routers growing into complex entities. Some switching devices have hundreds of ports, and each port supports tens of counters. That makes it impossible for a monitoring application to show easily whether an interface behaves normally or which ones are the most congested or problematic.

The answer is a sorted, shorter list of the most significant interfaces, chosen by programmable criteria.
sections.eli5: When a building has hundreds of doors, nobody can watch them all. A top-few list tells you which doors to look at first.

sections.title: The SNMP Framework and MIB Structure
sections.content:
The memo describes the SNMP Management Framework as five components: an overall architecture, the Structure of Management Information (SMIv1 and SMIv2), message protocols (SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3), protocol operations, and a set of fundamental applications plus view-based access control. This MIB module is written in SMIv2, and an SMIv1 version can be produced by translation.

The module contains one group, interfaceTopNObjects. It holds one capability object, interfaceTopNCaps, and two tables: interfaceControlTable and interfaceTopNTable.
sections.eli5: The rules for talking to network gear already exist. This RFC just adds one new form to fill in and one new results sheet.

sections.title: Control Table and Reports
sections.content:
The control table is an RMON-style table used to create reports. A management station sets the report's duration, the number of interfaces wanted, the start time, and how the chosen variable is treated. Rows have an owner and a RowStatus object, and settings cannot be changed while the row is active.

interfaceTopNObjectVariable picks the variable to sample. Values 0 to 22 point to objects in IF-MIB, 23 to 37 to EtherLike-MIB, 38 to 55 to TOKENRING-MIB, 56 to 72 to RMON-MIB and 73 to 75 to BRIDGE-MIB. The agent advertises what it can sort by in interfaceTopNCaps.

Writing interfaceTopNTimeRemaining starts a collection; it counts down by one per second. Report entries are inaccessible while it is non-zero and become visible in interfaceTopNTable when it reaches zero. Setting it to zero while running aborts the report. The requested size defaults to 10, and the agent reports what it grants in interfaceTopNGrantedSize.

The result table lists interfaces in decreasing order of value, with index 1 for the highest. Interfaces whose value would be zero are not included.
sections.eli5: You fill in a form saying what to count, for how long and how many to list. When the timer hits zero, the ranked list appears, with the biggest number first.

sections.title: Sample Types and Normalization
sections.content:
interfaceTopNObjectSampleType has three settings. absoluteValue(1) copies the variable's value directly. deltaValue(2) stores the difference between the current and the last sample. bandwidthPercentage(3) divides the octets sent over an interval by the octets that represent 100% bandwidth and multiplies by 1000, giving a value in tenths of a percent from 0 to 1000. The RFC says this suits octet counters and is not recommended for packet or error counters.

Normalization lets interfaces of different speeds be compared. When interfaceTopNNormalizationReq is true, the sampled value is multiplied by the normalization factor divided by the interface's effective speed. In the RFC's example, a factor of 1000000000 multiplies deltas by 100 for 10 Mbps interfaces and by 10 for 100 Mbps interfaces, and leaves 1 Gbps interfaces unchanged. Normalization cannot be true with the bandwidth percentage type, and it must be false when the effective speed from ifSpeed is zero.

Results are in interfaceTopNValue (Gauge32) for 32-bit objects and bandwidth percentages, and interfaceTopNValue64 for 64-bit counters.
sections.eli5: A garden hose and a fire hose carry different amounts of water. Normalizing is like scaling so you can fairly say which one is working hardest for its size.

sections.title: How the Design Evolved
sections.content:
The RMON working group first charted a document to find the most congested ports quickly. The first version used objects in tables indexed by an InterfaceIndex (from RFC 2863), which simplified the search and result table but limited the method to interface parameters.

At a meeting in Adelaide in March 2000, the group decided to try a more generic usrTopN function that could sort variables from tables with any index, at the cost of extra processing and checking by the agent. At an interim meeting in San Francisco in May 2000 it dropped that approach for this phase, partly because a normalization factor is hard to define generically and the group did not want applications to supply a scaling factor for every instance.
sections.eli5: The authors first tried a bigger idea that could rank anything. It turned out too hard to do fairly, so they kept the simpler version that ranks network interfaces.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access may be sensitive, and allowing SET operations in a non-secure environment can harm network operations. The RFC also names interfaceTopNDataSourceIndex and interfaceTopNValue as objects that may hold sensitive information, so even GET access should be controlled, and values possibly encrypted in transit.

SNMPv1 on its own is not a secure environment. The RFC recommends considering SNMPv3 security, specifically the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model. Because SNMP access control works on MIB views, the variable-selection object may only be writable in views that can read every object on the probe.
sections.eli5: The counters can reveal what a network is doing, so only trusted people should be allowed to look at them or change the settings.

viz.caption: SAMPLE TYPES FOR THE SELECTED VARIABLE

items.label: absoluteValue
items.desc: The variable's value is copied directly into the result.

items.label: deltaValue
items.desc: The previous sample is subtracted from the current value and the difference is stored.

items.label: bandwidthPercentage
items.desc: Octets sent over the interval divided by the 100% bandwidth octets, times 1000, in tenths of a percent.
